messages.author: 9d5350458e6c3801
messages.subject: Can I sample this way?
parts:
Dear Help,
 
I want to do sampling for my model, saying
y ~ intercept + z*beta + f(i,spde)
where z is some covariate(s) and f(i,spde) is the SPDE random effect.

After searching for a while, I found there is a function inla.posterior.sample() that can sample from the posteriors which is great! However, I wonder if the sampling procedure can be controlled by some (hyper)parameters, such as beta, kappa, tau, etc? What I suppose now is as follows and I am not sure if that makes sense..
 
1. sample random samples from the posteriors of intercept, beta, kappa, tau, saying b0, b, k, t..
2. sample from the Gaussian field x~N(0,Q) where Q is defined by kappa and tau, pluged in k and t from step 1. and calculate the Ax to be the GF values at corresponding locations (A=inla.spde.make.A(..)) 
3. add the terms together, y = b0 + z*b + Ax which is one sample..
 
I am feeling that there must be something wrong but I am not clear.. for example, the posterior of the random effect x should be not N(0,Q(kappa, tau)) ?  Anyway, what I need is by sampling only a few parameters (the values of the parameters can be controlled by users), I can get reasonable samples of the response variable... Is that possible?
 
Thanks a lot in advance!
 
Best regards,
Eridk

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can I sample this way?
parts:
On 05/05/14 11:23, Eridk Poliruyt wrote:
> Dear Help,
> I want to do sampling for my model, saying
> y ~ intercept + z*beta + f(i,spde)
> where z is some covariate(s) and f(i,spde) is the SPDE random effect.
>
> After searching for a while, I found there is a function
> inla.posterior.sample() that can sample from the posteriors which is
> great! However, I wonder if the sampling procedure can be controlled by
> some (hyper)parameters, such as beta, kappa, tau, etc?

The model consists of parameters kappa, tau and observation precision
(jointly called theta, for historical and other reasons called
hyper-parameters in R-INLA; I tend to call them simply parameters),
and latent Gaussian variables b0, beta, and {x(1),...x(m)} (the spde).
inla.posterior.sample() samples from the joint posterior of _all_ of
these, including b0, beta, {x(.)}, and all of the theta:s.

> What I suppose
> now is as follows and I am not sure if that makes sense..
> 1. sample random samples from the posteriors of intercept, beta, kappa,
> tau, saying b0, b, k, t..
> 2. sample from the Gaussian field x~N(0,Q) where Q is defined by kappa
> and tau, pluged in k and t from step 1. and calculate the Ax to be the
> GF values at corresponding locations (A=inla.spde.make.A(..))

That will produce a sample from the model for x itself, taken under the
posterior distribution for its parameters, which is not the same thing
as a sample from its own posterior distribution. The point of
inla.posterior.sample() is precisely to produce samples from the joint
posterior for all the unknowns in the model, so it will do the right
thing.

> 3. add the terms together, y = b0 + z*b + Ax which is one sample..
> I am feeling that there must be something wrong but I am not clear.. for
> example, the posterior of the random effect x should be not N(0,Q(kappa,
> tau)) ?

Right, Q(kappa,tau) is _not_ the posterior precision for x (in fact, the
posterior for x|y,theta isn't even Gaussian if y is non-Gaussian).
See the GMRF book by Rue and Held (2005) for details of what the
posterior precision for x|y,theta is.

> Anyway, what I need is by sampling only a few parameters (the
> values of the parameters can be controlled by users), I can get
> reasonable samples of the response variable... Is that possible?
> Thanks a lot in advance!

Do you mean that you want to fix certain parameters to known values, and
estimate the rest (and then produce samples from that posterior)?
That can be done in several ways, the details sometimes depending on
precisely which parameters you want to keep fixed.

Finn L

messages.author: 9d5350458e6c3801
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can I sample this way?
parts:
Thanks a lot!
  
I am not clear about the term *observation precision*, what is that?
Basically, what I want to do is to reduce the dimension of the random samples. We are doing sensitivity analysis of a climate model, basically each random sample lead to one climate model run which is time consuming. And from the experimental design, we can consider the values at each location as a parameter in the input space of the climate model and then we can design simulation only on a few combination of the "input parameters" (not your parameters in R-INLA). But the random samples are drawn on quite a lot of locations so that the number of "input parameters" are so big. So I wonder if we can do this: by sampling only a few parameters, and based on these parameters the random sample can be drawn so that the problem can be transfered from the random samples at many locations to only a few parameters so that experimental design can be affordable. 
 
Thanks!
Eridk
